title: The smoke
hook: watch for the day the sky brings a visible smoke (44:10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, baraka, the night the Qur'an came down, a night better than a thousand months. Did you find your minute in the dark, and what did the quiet sound like? Day five hundred seventy-three.
screen: `A NIGHT BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.`

segments.voice: A man in a starving city looks up, and between him and the sky he sees something like smoke. Hold that picture; it comes from an early report. The surah we opened yesterday takes its name from one word in its tenth verse: dukhan, smoke. And the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did not agree about what that smoke was. One of them thought it had already happened, in a hungry time in Mecca. Others thought it was still coming.

Here is the verse, in plain words: watch for the day when the sky brings a smoke plain to see. The next verse says it will cover the people, a painful torment, and the people cry out to their Lord to remove it. Then the surah says it will be lifted for a little while, and they will return to their ways. Two readings come down from the earliest generation. The first is from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. He said the Quraysh of Mecca resisted the Prophet so hard that he prayed against them, and a famine came, until people ate bones and carrion. A man would look up at the sky and see something like smoke between himself and it, from the hunger. Then the Meccans asked for relief, it came, and they went back to what they had been doing, just as the verses describe. For Ibn Mas'ud, the smoke was a past event. The second reading, linked to 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, says the smoke is one of the great signs before the Last Day. A hadith in Sahih Muslim lists ten signs before the Hour, and the smoke is among them. Some scholars hold both: a smoke that came, and a smoke still to come. What stays the same in every reading is the shape. Something in the sky makes people afraid. They cry out. Relief comes. And then, very quickly, they forget they ever asked. The surah isn't only describing a catastrophe. It's describing how short human memory can be once the air clears.
screen: `WATCH FOR THE VISIBLE SMOKE.` · `IBN MAS'UD: A FAMINE IN MECCA.` · `OTHERS: A SIGN BEFORE THE HOUR.` · `THEY ASK, IT LIFTS, THEY FORGET.`

segments.voice: The practice is simple: notice the air you breathe. Sit, and breathe in through the nose. Feel how cool it is on the way in, how warm on the way out. You didn't earn this air. You didn't ask for it this morning. Think of a day the air was bad: smoke from a fire, a stuffy room, a cold that blocked everything. Then come back to this breath, clear. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for the air itself. The bell holds the time.
The smoke. Dukhan: the sign in 44:10, read by Ibn Mas'ud as a famine haze in Mecca, and by others as a sign still to come. Today's word.
Your line: a sign in the sky. Today, look up once, at clear sky or gray, and remember one time relief came and you forgot to say thank you. Day five hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Muslims read Ad-Dukhan as part of the Qur'an's warnings; commentators teach both readings of the smoke, the famine in Mecca and a sign before the Last Day.

match.prompt: two readings of the smoke — tap the pairs.

in the verses, the relief is followed by forgetting
the smoke lifts for a while, and the people return to their ways.

fork.setup: you're a Meccan in the famine years. the sky looks like smoke. what does the surah say people do?
options: they cry out for relief, then forget once it comes.
fork.reveal: the verses describe people asking for the torment to be lifted, and returning to their ways when it is.

original.note: Arabic: smoke; the word that names surah 44.

trapdoor: what you thought: smoke, like from a fire.
what it means: a sign in the sky that covers people, read as a famine haze or a sign before the Last Day.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari records Ibn Mas'ud's famine reading; Muslim's hadith of ten signs before the Hour names the smoke; some scholars accept both.

Editor review: the 44:10 quotation was not in Pickthall's exact wording (his text includes an inserted '(O Muhammad)' and may read 'heaven'), so it is now paraphrased with quoted: null; the hook's general claim about hunger and eyesight replaced with the image from Ibn Mas'ud's report; 'years of it' and 'many scholars' softened; the Thursday-night recitation (weak hadith) cut from howItsDone.
